catalog_quote: L’accent est en général sur la pénultième syllabe, quand le mot en contient deux ou trois; sur l’antépénultième, quand le mot a plus de trois syllabes. Cependant α) les mots composés gardent souvent les deux accents des composants, tout en forçant un peu plus celui du mot principal. Ex. akufálu, dáilabílabi. β) Les mots se terminant par une diphtongue descendante, autre que l’-ai du suffixe circonstanciel, y reportent leur accent, ex. kabói̯, udái̯, mais banúai̯. γ) Les suffixes de relation intransitive na, ka, mu̯i, -tsi (v. ci-dessous) transportent l’accent à la pénultième syllabe. Ex. adavána, adaváka, adavámu̯i, adavátsi, mais adávau, adávamu et adavamái̯. [p. 986:] ... à la 3e pers. sing. ce suffixe est souvent omis, quand le verbe n’a pas d’autre suffixe, et n’est pas au passé. Ex. oyame boloma fe alá le chien mordra le porc. Remarquez cependant l’accent sur la dernière syllabe. .…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kuni (kuni1263, Oceanic, Central Province PNG) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Francard et al. 2001 'L'accent belge: Mythes et réalités', is a Glottolog machine mis-assignment (the saved BibTeX record says lgcode 'Kuni [kse] (computerized assignment from \"mythes\")'); it is a chapter on the Belgian French regional accent and irrelevant, priority none. The best first-hand stress statement is Egidi 1913 (Anthropos 8, p. 983; already on file at from an earlier pass, re-read and verified against the page image): accent generally penultimate in 2-3-syllable words and antepenultimate in longer words, with compound, final-falling-diphthong and suffix-conditioned exceptions, plus accent alternations marking verb forms (pp. 986-987). Pawley 1975 (on file) is silent on stress. Jones 2020 (Oceanic Linguistics 59, doi:10.1353/ol.2020.0004) remains unread behind Project MUSE; low priority for stress. web lookups and Crossref/Glottolog records were used instead. in the audit folder was appended with a date -u stamped sweep entry.

new_statements.quote: L'accent est en général sur la pénultième syllabe, quand le mot en contient deux ou trois; sur l'antépénultième, quand le mot a plus de trois syllabes. Cependant α) les mots composés gardent souvent les deux accents des composants, tout en forçant un peu plus celui du mot principal. Ex. akufálu, dáilabílabi. β) Les mots se terminant par une diphtongue descendante, autre que l'-ai du suffixe circonstanciel, y reportent leur accent, ex. kabói̯, udái̯, mais banúai̯. γ) Les suffixes de relation intransitive na, ka, mu̯i, -tsi (v. ci-dessous) transportent l'accent à la pénultième syllabe. Ex. adavána, adaváka, adavámu̯i, adavátsi, mais adávau, adávamu et adavamái̯.
new_statements.translation: The accent is in general on the penultimate syllable when the word contains two or three syllables; on the antepenultimate when the word has more than three syllables. However (a) compound words often keep both accents of their components, while making that of the principal word somewhat stronger, e.g. akufálu, dáilabílabi; (b) words ending in a falling diphthong, other than the -ai of the circumstantial suffix, carry their accent on it, e.g. kabói, udái, but banúai; (c) the intransitive-relation suffixes na, ka, mui, -tsi shift the accent to the penultimate syllable, e.g. adavána, adaváka, adavámui, adavátsi, but adávau, adávamu and adavamái.
new_statements.citation: Egidi, Vincenzo M. 1913. Mythes et légendes des Kuni, British New-Guinea. Anthropos 8: 978-1009.
new_statements.locator: p. 983, section 'II. La langue kuni' (PDF page 6 of the extract = page 1057 of the full-volume scan); further remarks p. 986
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check:, extract page 6 = Anthropos 8 p. 983 (running head 'Mythes et Légendes des Kuni, British New-Guinea. 983'), verified against the 200-dpi render : the paragraph 'L'accent est en général sur la pénultième syllabe, quand le mot en contient deux ou trois; sur l'antépénultième, quand le mot a plus de trois syllabes. Cependant α)... akufálu, dáilabílabi. β)... kabói̯, udái̯, mais banúai̯. γ)... adavána, adaváka, adavámu̯i, adavátsi, mais adávau, adávamu et adavamái̯.' is there word for word, diacritics included (the extracted text layer garbles the acutes, the image does not). The p. 986 remarks are also as reported (extract page 9): 'à la 3e pers. sing. ce suffixe est souvent omis..…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is penultimate in di- and trisyllables and antepenultimate in words of four or more syllables; a word-final falling diphthong attracts the accent (except the circumstantial suffix -ai); certain verbal suffixes (na, ka, mui, tsi) pull the accent onto the (new) penult while others (-au, -mu, -mai) do not; compounds retain the accent of each member with the head's stronger. On p. 986 Egidi adds that a 3sg transitive verb with the suffix dropped keeps accent on the final syllable, and that 'neutral' (intransitive) vs active forms are often distinguished by an accent shift (a uíka 'I put myself in' vs a uiká 'I put in'), i.e. accent has some morphological load.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only for compounds: both members keep their accent, the principal word's being somewhat stronger (akufálu, dáilabílabi).
new_statements.exceptions: Final falling diphthongs take the accent (kabói̯, udái̯) except circumstantial -ai (banúai̯); suffixes na/ka/mu̯i/tsi shift accent to penult, -au/-mu/-mai̯ do not (adávau, adávamu, adavamái̯); 3sg verb with omitted transitive suffix is final-accented; active vs neutral verb pairs differ by accent (a uíka / a uiká).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in the Dilava variety as transcribed by a resident missionary (1904-1907); 'en général' hedges the rule; the antepenult clause for 4+-syllable words makes this a length-conditioned penult/antepenult system rather than pure fixed penult, and the verb remarks show some morphological conditioning. Accent is marked with acute on cited forms throughout the sketch and texts.
new_statements.identity_note: Egidi describes the Kuni spoken at Dilava (his Sacred Heart mission station on the upper St Joseph/Aroa, 1904-1907), explicitly 'la langue parlée à Dilava', and notes dialect differences elsewhere (Devadeva replaces k by aspiration; right-bank groups Idoido, Maimai, Yaifa shift several consonants; Inauveida tinged with Pokau). This is the same language as Glottolog kuni1263 / ISO kse (modern centre Bakoiudu). Caution: Glottolog's kse bibliography also lists R. Fumey's SIL literacy booklets, which belong to Kuni-Boazi [kvg] of Western Province, a different (non-Austronesian) language.

new_statements.translation: The accent is in general on the penultimate syllable when the word has two or three syllables; on the antepenultimate when the word has more than three syllables. However (a) compound words often keep the two accents of their components, while strengthening somewhat that of the main word, e.g. akufálu, dáilabílabi. (b) Words ending in a falling diphthong, other than the -ai of the circumstantial suffix, carry their accent on it, e.g. kabói, udái, but banúai. (c) The intransitive-relation suffixes na, ka, mui, -tsi (see below) move the accent to the penultimate syllable, e.g. adavána, adaváka, adavámui, adavátsi, but adávau, adávamu and adavamái.
new_statements.citation: Egidi, Vincenzo M. (1913). Mythes et Légendes des Kuni, British New-Guinea. Anthropos 8: 978-1009 (grammar sketch 'II. La langue kuni', pp. 981-988).
new_statements.reading: Default word accent is penultimate in 2-3-syllable words and antepenultimate in longer words (a length-conditioned rule, in effect the third syllable from the start for 3-syllable words and the antepenult beyond that), with lexical/morphological exceptions: compounds retain secondary accents on their members, word-final falling diphthongs attract the accent (final-position accent), and certain suffixes re-anchor accent to the penult while others (au, amu, -mái) do not. Egidi also notes final accent on an unsuffixed 3sg verb form (p. 986) and accent alternation marking the neuter vs active verb form (pp. 986-987). A trained missionary sketch from 1913 with accent marks throughout the texts; the only first-hand stress description of Kuni found. Language not in the catalog; if entered, this would be its deciding source (coding suggestion: penultimate default with antepenultimate in 4+ syllable words, plus lexical/final-diphthong exceptions).

sources.note: Only openly accessible modern linguist's note on Kuni grammar (fieldwork c. 1981 plus Egidi and Eschlimann). Silent on the general word-stress rule but states that the present-imperfect is marked by word stress on the subject-marking prefix (è-mai 'is coming' vs i-mai 'came'), 'not always observed with polysyllabic verb words' -- a grammatical stress alternation to record alongside Egidi's penult default.
